items.author: SRS0=iwSH=HZ=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content: Fortunately, the largest counties like Harris County, Dallas, Collin County, Tarrant County – the counties with the largest backlog of registration applications – are well-resourced. They have people and expanded resources so they are actually getting through these applications really fast. The numbers, of course, were large, and people were panicking initially. But based on conversations that I had with those election officials and the type of technology that they have on their hands, they're gonna get these through. The problem is the smaller counties, the ones that are not as well resourced, the ones that have one or two staffers working. There are counties out there that really their elections department is a one man show, believe it or not, and so those counties are the ones that are going to be really working day and night to try to process these.

items.title: Free ebook from Chicago: Plundered Skulls and Stolen Spirits
items.author: 554127793.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
Who owns the past and the objects that physically connect us to history? And who has the right to decide this ownership, particularly when the objects are sacred or, in the case of skeletal remains, human? Is it the museums that care for the objects or the communities whose ancestors made them? These questions are at the heart of , an unflinching insider account by a leading curator who has spent years learning how to balance these controversial considerations.

Five decades ago, Native American leaders launched a crusade to force museums to return their sacred objects and allow them to rebury their kin. Today, hundreds of tribes use the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act to help them recover their looted heritage from museums across the country. As senior curator of anthropology at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, Chip Colwell has navigated firsthand the questions of how to weigh the religious freedom of Native Americans against the academic freedom of scientists and whether the emptying of museum shelves elevates human rights or destroys a common heritage. This book offers his personal account of the process of repatriation, following the trail of four objects as they were created, collected, and ultimately returned to their sources: a sculpture that is a living god, the scalp of a massacre victim, a ceremonial blanket, and a skeleton from a tribe considered by some to be extinct. These specific stories reveal a dramatic process that involves not merely obeying the law, but negotiating the blurry lines between identity and morality, spirituality and politics.

Things, like people, have biographies. Repatriation, Colwell argues, is a difficult but vitally important way for museums and tribes to acknowledge that fact—and heal the wounds of the past while creating a respectful approach to caring for these rich artifacts of history.

items.title: Who’s That Guy? 2026 MLB postseason edition
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
There’s no one on the Dodgers at this point who deserves "Who’s That Guy?" treatment. If they have a new face in the mix at all, it will be highly touted prospect Josue De Paula, off the bench. And yet they have the ultimate example of a player who makes viewers utter the question.

Kiké Hernández is pretty solidly this generation’s most disproportionate October scene-stealer — he’s That Guy in the same way as an actor with no starring credits but a hundred memorable bit character roles. He’s a player whose baseball fan Q score is entirely dependent on your postseason consumption.

All those roles have earned him serious screen time. Hernández has taken more postseason plate appearances (328) than all but eight players since his debut 11 years ago. In that playing time? He has been Good. His .826 OPS is 15th among the 49 hitters who have taken at least 150 trips to the plate in the same span — behind 13 guys for whom the Hall of Fame is or was at one point a reasonable possibility, and Randy Arozarena. He’s three points ahead of Aaron Judge.

Who’s that guy? He’s someone who has made the most of the biggest moments. Over and over. Everyone else on this list would be thrilled to join him, even just once.

The bulk of today’s newsletter is devoted to players who might make their names nationally known over the next month or so, who might go from unheralded to hero, from promising to the prince who was promised. Will I ever match the inaugural edition of this exercise from 2020, in which I picked out mostly anonymous, hotel-quarantined, push-up-performing, cowboy-boot-wearing Arozarena as a potential playoff difference-maker? Almost certainly not! But we press on anyway.

Thanks to The War On Drugs for creating a soundtrack specifically for this segment.

Victor Mesa Jr., Rays outfielder

Even after a pretty unimpeachable 98-win season to stun the competition in a rugged AL East, it’s understandable if the Rays lineup doesn’t jump out at you. Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz, Jonathan Aranda, trade deadline addition Liam Hicks, and then who?

Victor Mesa Jr., that’s who.

If you’d heard of Mesa prior to this year, it was probably as the second fiddle to his ballyhooed brother Victor Victor Mesa. The Marlins signed both of them out of Cuba back in 2018, but this Victor Mesa (singular, second of his name) surpassed his sibling and gradually worked his way up through the minors. The Rays got him in a trade in February, brought him up for his MLB debut in May and benefited as he established himself as a key piece of their lineup, batting .260 with 14 homers and nine steals in 79 games.

The postseason amps up the competition level. The precise contours of that shift are difficult to put under the microscope, but one is very apparent: A greater share of all pitches will be zipping in faster. Being able to handle premium velocity is not everything, but it’s a nice trait when push comes to shove in October, one shared by some of the era’s most durable postseason bats: Bryce Harper, Max Muncy, Yordan Alvarez, etc.

So I took note that, among all hitters who saw at least 75 pitches over 97 mph in 2026, Mesa registered the best results, slashing .412/.524/.941 with three long balls. He’s also coming in red hot, with a 184 wRC+ in September ranking as a top 15 mark in the majors.

Garrett Mitchell, Brewers outfielder

Let me put this as plainly as possible: Mitchell is an absolute athletic freak. If Statcast were sentient, it would be making googly eyes at him from across the bar.

The problem has been actualizing those physical gifts on the field. Mitchell might just be Byron Buxton Lite. At age 28, he finally played a full-ish season. It went pretty well! He homered 11 times, stole 14 bags and played good if unspectacular defense in center field. His hyperdrive swing is pretty locked into a path, perhaps hindering his ability to make contact and contributing to a high strikeout rate, but he also upped his walk rate and reached base at a .354 clip. Pretty useful!

Healthy and leading off for another dynamite Brewers team, there’s a good chance Mitchell throws up sparks.

Adrián Morejón, Padres pitcher

Mason Miller is the headliner in San Diego’s monster bullpen, but the left-handed Morejón is more than a supporting act. Over the past three years, Morejón has thrown more innings in relief than anyone in baseball, while also being one of the 10 most dominant arms working out of the bullpen, by Fielding Independent Pitching’s accounting of strikeouts, walks and homers.

If the Padres run into crucial moments before the eighth inning, expect Morejón (or Bradgley Rodriguez) to get the nod.

George Lombard Jr., Yankees shortstop

Since no one has ever gotten out over their skis about a young Yankees shortstop, I think it’s safe to dream on Lombard Jr. as he is thrust into the spotlight in pinstripes.

The 21-year-old major-league scion forced his way to the Bronx with power potential, a mature approach — on-base percentage across three minor-league levels: .411 — and defensive savvy. He understandably hasn’t mastered that approach at the big-league level just yet, but you can see flashes of his aptitude. Four hits and three runs against the Red Sox was a roaring start.

If he mans a solid shortstop and keeps his strikeouts in check, he’s going to have plaudits and expectations following him like paparazzi.

Tyler Mahle, Braves pitcher

Perhaps the under-the-radar deadline move of the year, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA for the Braves after running up a 5.13 mark for the Giants. Neither the great nor the bad was totally reflective of his efforts, but the 32-year-old has altered his formula a little since the deal, boosting his splitter usage to career highs.

His continued good form is wildly important for Atlanta’s hopes of advancing any further. It’s essentially Chris Sale, Mahle and then a blurred line between swingmen, openers and bulk guys. Even in an eventual loss, his seven strong innings in Wild Card Game 2 kept the Braves’ pitching corps strong enough to win Game 3.

If Mahle is asked to make the same bold stand against the Dodgers, he’ll have a chance to redefine his workmanlike career into something else entirely.

Hagen Smith, White Sox pitcher

With a time machine and a healthy appreciation for trickery, you could really mess with White Sox fans by going back to 2024 and telling them that their newest top five draft pick would start a postseason Game 1 within three years.

That statement is technically true now, as Smith opened their Wild Card Series romp over the Astros, but not yet spiritually accurate. The lefty has reached the majors as a reliever, with iffy command still hampering excellent stuff. Yet as he found his footing in the bullpen, he improved, throwing down MLB’s fifth-best strikeout rate in September.

He’s a boom or bust proposition, but nonetheless looks like one of the best options available to manager Will Venable. It’s first-round talent, something you don’t need a time machine to see.

Angel Martinez, Guardians outfielder

The Guardians, believe it or not, had the best second-half offense of any team remaining in the American League side of the bracket, per park-adjusted wRC+. Steven Kwan and Chase DeLauter were the biggest reasons for their run-scoring prowess, but the lineup is longer on threats than it might appear. Maybe.

Martinez was great down the stretch, batting .310/.346/.559 after Aug. 1, good for a 152 wRC+ that was “between Bryce Harper and Yordan Alvarez” good.

Did the underlying numbers support such production? No, no they did not. Martinez will swing at almost anything, but he does usually make contact, and he does usually scoop that contact into the air to the pull side. He is nothing if not a man of action, and sometimes that’s enough. ⚾️

An arbitrary Bandwagon fan ranking of the remaining teams

Every remaining team ranked by their attractiveness as a narrative foil for the Dodgers:

  1. Padres: Little brother bets his life savings he can jump his bike over the house into the pool, then somehow does it
  2. Brewers: What if Moneyball had a happy ending?
  3. White Sox: Downtrodden soul is suddenly emboldened by God
  4. Yankees: Old money reasserts dominance
  5. Rays: What if Moneyball had a sequel that had a happy ending?
  6. Guardians: Tortoise beats hare, but if speed were home runs or something
  7. Braves: Rival takes out more accomplished rival
  8. Dodgers: A true champion’s only competition comes from within

The 2026 Red Sox were bad, and then amazing, and then they were just … fine. And fine doesn’t tend to cut it in the playoffs. It did not cut it at Yankee Stadium this week, and the good feelings of their amazing win streak dissolved into rancor.

Chad Tracy, no longer just the interim manager, is in the loud, squishy muck of disappointment after the Red Sox let both games get away from them shortly after pulling their starting pitchers. Neither Payton Tolle in Game 1 nor Sonny Gray in Game 2 were winning their duels with Yankees aces Cam Schlittler and Max Fried, but their departures registered as early and preceded big Yankees hits.

After it all, the veteran Gray expressed his problem directly.

“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time,” Gray told reporters. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am. I think you can probably ask the (players), and they felt the same way.”

I don’t think either decision had a clear cut answer, though I admittedly preferred Gray over Erik Miller for a second straight day in Game 2. But any hope for a rational discussion of those nebulous, uncertain calculations was dashed when Willson Contreras said the magic words to summon Tired Baseball Discourse, complaining that players “have computers telling you what to do.”

This should blow over. It would be more concerning if a clubhouse full of players  frustrated and a little angry minutes after their season ended. But this being Boston, and the tone of these comments being pointed, it also seems two days in the Bronx could scrub the Red Sox all the way back to April, to the offseason, to the raised eyebrows and skeptical glances directed at top baseball executive Craig Breslow and his front office.

It will all be different come spring, yet it might not feel much different until there’s a more powerful memory to override these repeated shortcomings. This resilient summer felt like it might be just that, until it didn’t.

The Padres chewed up the Cubs and spat them out, much to the delight of a raucous crowd at Petco Park. Fernando Tatis Jr. blasted a homer on the first pitch of the bottom of the first inning in Game 1, the ball slipping just over the glove of a soaring Pete Crow-Armstrong, and it really just devolved from there.

Padres starter Michael King sliced and diced them in Game 1, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh. Then, as the fans chanted the Don Orsillo home run call “Holy Sheets” in Game 2 …

Gavin Sheets complied. And the Cubs never got off the mat.

Despite the emergence of Crow-Armstrong as the obvious NL MVP, a true superstar, the Cubs are teetering over an abyss of an offseason with a bevy of impending free agents and a dearth of apparent answers to the resulting holes.

Re-signing and/or replacing all of the talent sloughing off this roster will be hugely expensive. The Cubs don't have great alternatives, though, given the state of their farm system. Their margin for error next year is thinner than it would have been if they'd been less aggressive at the deadline, too, as Brett Bateman (outfield), Moisés Ballesteros (DH) and Jefferson Rojas(infield) all could have been reinforcements for the roster if they hadn't been dealt away. The front office recognized the importance of capitalizing on the year they were getting from Crow-Armstrong and on the last prime-adjacent years of Bregman, Swanson, Happ, Suzuki and more. They pushed in their chips. After Wednesday night, it sure feels like they lost the hand, but playing it was the brave (and perhaps the only) thing to do.

It’s still too early to draw conclusions about the postseason’s effect on challenge strategy — or challenge emotions — but the tension is clearly high.

“What we’ve made clear,” Venable, the White Sox manager, told The Athletic, “the worst thing that can happen is that we get to the end of the game, we have two challenges left and we’ve missed a bunch of opportunities to use our challenges.”

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Filter or funnel
items.author: bounces+r8ummxv832soh3p8536c2hdx2548ds7h376k@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about how to decide what news to share with your team and when to share it.​

If you share every whiff of bad news with your team, they may become paranoid and paralyzed, preventing them from doing their work. But of course you

need to share bad news sometimes.​

And what about good news? Should you just share everything you can? Sharing unconfirmed rumors could be counter-productive, but you do get a boost when you

share some good news.

So how do you decide what to share and when to share it?

Use the "Filter or funnel" framework to make those decisions easier and more strategic:

One of the most challenging aspects of leadership is deciding what information to share with your team and when to share it. In general, you should over-communicate so everyone is on the same page as often as possible, but you shouldn’t communicate to your team.

Here’s a rubric to help you decide what to communicate:

You are privy to a lot more of your organization’s inner workings and machinations than your team is. And while you want them to be synced up, you don’t want them to be paranoid or possibly paralyzed by fear and uncertainty. You also don’t want them to be excited about something coming down the pike only for them to be disappointed when it doesn’t come to fruition.

When thinking about filtering, your threshold for sharing potential bad news should be high.

Here are some questions you might ask before sharing bad news with your team:

    If the bad news is confirmed or at least extremely likely and it will affect your team, then you might want to get out ahead of it. If they can help prevent the bad thing from happening or at least prepare better, then you might enlist them once they understand the stakes and how they can help.

    When thinking about , be generous. Once you confirm the good news, then lean toward sharing it unless it may be a distraction or might better be saved as a surprise. Sharing good news is a way to encourage your team, bolster morale, and counterbalance the daily frustrations that come along.

items.title: Searching for answers after a "disappointing" Royals season
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
The Royals held their annual wrap-up press conference on Wednesday. In a year where they expectation was playoffs and the reality was 69 wins, this was a grim autopsy on a season that manager Matt Quatraro said was “frustrating” and General Manager JJ Picollo termed “disappointing.” I would concur with both of those adjectives. Entering the season, expectations were high. It was obvious fairly early on that they wouldn't come close to meeting those expectations.

As usual, I'll highlight some of the key moments from the press conference by quoting Picollo or Quatraro. Then, I'll add a little analysis for my take.

We start with the news that broke on Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt will not be in the Royals dugout next year. Funny…nobody really knows how to categorize what the Royals did with Zumwalt. He didn’t get reassigned necessarily. He is still the Senior Director of Hitting Performance. He just lost the title of Hitting Coach. His responsibilities have shifted? His duties have become more focused?

Whatever happened, according to Picollo, the shift in focus to the minor leagues for Zumwalt was part of the long-term plan when he joined the major league staff.

“This was something that was anticipated the day he was brought to the major leagues. He came up in the middle of ’22. Alec had a tremendous history with all of the guys that are most of the guys on our team, but the core that you all have seen play here for two or three years. So it was important to have him on the staff when we did, and he did a good job.”

According to Picollo, Zumwalt leaving his hitting coach role in 2026 was part of the motivation behind adding Connor Dawson and Marcus Thames last year to the staff as hitting coaches along with Zumwalt. They serve as continuity as Zumwalt moves out of the dugout. And Picollo says the club will fill the spot Zumwalt is vacating. He anticipates that will be done sometime in October.

Seems like a lot of dominios the front office was trying to align. According to Picollo, he and Zumwalt had the “is it time to return to the minors?” talk in the last couple of winters.

“Alec and I had a conversation to end of every season about is this the time to go back to the minor leagues. So this is really about succession planning. And there was succession plans in place. And there's a lot of confidence in what Alec did as a minor league coordinator and even some of the things he did in the major leagues...And the truth of the matter, he's good. He's a good hitting coach.”

You may disagree with Picollo’s assessment of Zumwalt and, honestly, I’m not sure where I land. I don’t think he’s as terrible as a segment of the fanbase would have you believe. But the results are the results and, as I showed yesterday, they haven’t been good enough.

From what I could glean, Dawson and Thames will be co-leads, so to speak.

“As we get deeper into this offseason with Connor and Marcus, we'll hear more about their ideas. As assistants, they don't get to make the final call. Now those two will work together, and we'll find out more about what changes they may want to make.”

I had heard rumblings that the belief in the organization is that the improved offense over the season was due to Thames and Dawson making inroads with players. Building relationships takes time. If that was truly the case, the progress made was tangible.

A co-lead position is an interesting alignment where you have to coaches with very different backgrounds having an equal say. I don’t think the Royals would do this if they didn’t already have a good working relationship. Maybe this is the case where you don't really need a lead so to speak, but a couple of different voices for players when they're searching to unlock something. Still, it seems like this could sideways if there isn’t rock-solid alignment. Worth a shot, I suppose. They had to do something.

Picollo opened the presser noting that not only would Zumwalt not be returning to the dugout, but almost the entire major league medical staff—Head Athletic Trainer Kyle Turner, Assistant Athletic Trainer Chris DeLucia and Major League Rehab Coordinator Jeff Blum—would be leaving the club. Also moving to a minor league role is Melissa Lambert who was Director of Behaviorial Science.

This feels pretty seismic. Turner had been with the Royals for 17 years. DeLucia was with the team for 20 years and Blum was here for 19 years. The trio had all been in their current positions for five seasons. Lambert is returning to a focus on the minor leagues after four seasons in her role in the dugout. She’s been with the team since 2020.

Picollo on the cashiering of the major league medical staff:

“The way to look at that, most of those injuries there you have an idea going into it that there's an indicator that somebody may not have 10 years left three years left whatever and there were some indicators with some of our pitchers. You just don't want it to all happen at once… We try to do our best to prevent injuries. I think what we want to move to is a little more efficient way of getting guys back on the field. We've had some guys that haven't had surgeries that missed a significant amount of time. This is where I think the different departments all have to work together.”

I believe what Picollo is referring to about indicators is that pitcher injuries aren’t usually sudden. It’s something that teams are aware of where they try to manage the situation and milk as many innings out of their arms they can. And then there’s the rehab situation. Clearly, the Royals were not happy with the length of time some of these players needed to return to the field.

The thing that really stuck with me about the injuries from the 2026 season was how it seemed as though the Royals often dithered when making the call whether or not to put a player on the IL. They often played short-handed due to their indecisiveness. It was odd.

According to Sportrac, the Royals lost 1,796 days to the IL in 2026. That’s about the middle of the pack in the majors. For reference, though, the Royals lost just 994 days to the IL in 2024. Either way, in 2026 there were a lot of injuries and a lot of missed days.

Picollo was asked about how the Royals will address the avoiding another slow start in 2027 like the one that doomed them this year. The Royals were 15 games under .500 and 11 games out of first place in the AL Central on May 31. The record was the culmination of a March and April where they went 12-19 and followed that up with a May where they were even worse at 10-18.

“One thing I've thought about, and I know Q thinks about a lot, we come out of Arizona, which is a very offensive environment. So what's in your mind coming out is “hit”. And then the reality is you come here and it's cold. You go somewhere else and it's raining and sleeting. You don't have ideal conditions. But how do we combat that?…There's no magic formula for it. You just have to try to prepare. I do think, not just the Kansas City Royals, but I think there were several teams across baseball that were impacted by the WBC. We didn't have our team in spring training…We know all the players from the Royals that played. They did well. They were a national story. But when we got back together, it was like beginning of March again. But it was time to go. It was a regular season.”

I get it. The ball jumps in Arizona in Spring Training. It’s quite a different environment when the regular season starts in Kansas City the last week of March. And they did have plenty of players at the World Baseball Classic. Except the above statement feels like thin gruel given that those issues were often the same for every single team in the league. And the supposed hangover from the WBC and the shift from Arizona to colder weather lasted for a long time. Two months!

It just feels flimsy to point to those two things as factors in the team not performing up to expectations. I couldn't tell you why it happened, but I do know having your closer serve up a walkoff grand slam in the second game of the season followed by slow starts from several key offensive players followed by the buildup of injuries to the rotation and the general underperformance from the bullpen certainly seemed to snowball as the early weeks moved by. These sorts of things happen. Usually not all of them at once, but they happen. To point at having Spring Training in Arizona and the WBC as reasons seems a bit farfetched.

An area of focus this winter will be the bullpen. Obviously. Picollo noted that the Royals have been in the top five in spending on their bullpen over the last three years. He also acknowledged that splashing the cash on relievers, who are naturally finicky, may not be the best use of resources.:

“There's other ways to match up. And neutral relievers, neutral split relievers, left-on-left guys, guys that dominate right-handers, which is not usually the one you need the most of. There's different ways to do it, different arm slots. If you look at some of the acquisitions we had in the latter part of this year, we had some guys who were straight power, where we want to refine their command, and some guys are different arm slot guys. Let's see how that works for us.

Now it's a matter of just trying to put it all together. There's not a clear definitive answer on how to put a bullpen together, but I think the variety of different looks, different stuff, type of relievers is the way we're probably going to go.”

As for the closer, Picollo said they didn’t have anyone they were focused on for that role in 2027. They don’t think that they have one currently on the roster. I believe if it’s anyone, it’s Lucas Erceg. Especially if he can bottle those 100 mph fastballs. He was a completely different pitcher when he returned from Triple-A. Dare I say, closer-esque.

As for the position players, Picollo said Jac Caglianone will stay in right field and Vinnie Pasquantino is the primary first baseman going forward. He said that a focus will be finding more production—and better defense from left and center field. Carson Roccaforte, coming off a 30/30 season between Double and Triple-A has earned a look in center. It kind of makes me wonder if they’ll tender a contract to Kyle Isbel. He earned $2.7 million in 2026 and is eligible for arbitration the for the third time. He doesn’t break the bank, but his offensive degraded to the point that his defense couldn’t compensate. And his defense took a step back due to his foot issues.

The Royals lineup, as Picollo noted, is a bit left-handed heavy. They will be looking for balance. I kind of doubt they’d play the free agent market for a center fielder. Maybe Roccaforte has pushed his way to the front. For left field, there are a couple of right-handed hitters who will be available in the open market. Randy Arozarena is one, but he would command some dollars. Taylor Ward is another option, one that would be less expensive. He did well starting the season in Baltimore but then cratered after he was dealt to Seattle. Sliding down the scale, Ian Happ would be an even less expensive option. All three players are in their early 30s.

A couple of quick hits to wrap:

  • After opening the season with nine pitchers they felt could slot into the starting rotation and finishing the year with just three of those guys healthy, Picollo will never take starting pitching depth for granted.
  • Daniel Lynch IV has earned the opportunity to compete for a role in the rotation.
  • Picollo expects the Royals will pick up the option on Tony Gonsolin.
  • It doesn’t sound as if the Royals will be talking contract extensions with Jac Caglianone and Carter Jensen this winter. They’ll wait until they have two full years of service time before they open those talks.
  • Picollo is open to making trades to add to the roster, but he’s looking for major league talent. Not prospects. The goal is to win now.

Overall, a typical end of the season wrap from Picollo and Quatraro. I realize I didn't pull any Q quotes but he said a few things that I'll look into a little deeper in the coming days. Otherwise, it feels like the focus is on the right things going forward in addressing the injuries and rehab time to get players back on the field, along with shuffling the hitting coaches. The upcoming lockout will also play a factor in how the Royals move once the postseason wraps up.

This is a pivotal offseason for the Royals. After the shortcomings in 2025 and the absolute failure of 2026, they have to get it right for 2027.

items.title: Zumwalt out as Royals hitting coach
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
The Royals press conference to wrap the 2026 season is later on Wednesday. That didn't prevent news about the on-field staff from coming out on Tuesday. Ken Rosenthal at The Athletic had the scoop: The Royals were removing hitting coach Alec Zumwalt from the dugout.

Zumwalt just completed his 15th season with the Royals. He has been the Senior Director of Hitting Performance since 2021. He added hitting coach to his duties on May 16, 2022, replacing Terry Bradshaw.

Zumwalt came under quite a bit of fire as the offense seemed to regress across the board in 2025 and the Royals faded from the playoff race. The cracks started to show in September of 2024. The fire didn't abate in the early going in 2026 as an underperforming offense in the first two months of the season was part of the Royals three ring circus of baseballing frustrations.

Despite the early struggles, the Royals offense ran surprisingly close to league average for most of the 2026 season. They had a good April where they collectively hit .240/.322/.389 which was exactly in line with league average production. The nadir was the following month. In May the Royals hit .228/.294/.356, which was an 82 OPS+. That was abysmal. But they recovered and posted well the rest of the year. From Baseball Reference, we can see the Royals offense was fairly steady once they got past May:

Individually, Jac Caglianone really broke out this summer. He was the AL Player of the Month for August. Carter Jensen had an amazing season, building off his impressive cup of coffee from 2025. That culminated with an AL Player of the Month award for September. (More on that in a moment.) If you’re going to put the hitting coach on blast for underperforming players, you have to dole out some credit when the cornerstones of your organization flourish.

This is a results-based business. On offense, the results could be measured by the amount of runs scored. Here's how the Royals have done over the last five seasons in runs scored per game, along with their rank in the majors.

2026 - 4.26 R/G (22nd)2025 - 4.02 R/G (26th)2023 - 4.17 R/G (23rd)

The 2024 season looks like an extreme outlier but 2026 feels like a step forward. Since overall league offensive production varies from season to season, a full table from FanGraphs helps show how the Royals have done in regards to the league.

A reminder that wRC+ is Weighted Runs Created which is kind of a catch-all of offensive performance relative to the league. The league average is always 100. A number above 100 is above league average. Below 100 is below league average. In the Zumwalt hitting coach era, the Royals have run consistently below league average with their strongest years being 2024 and 2026.

Look at the raw numbers in the table above. The Royals posted their best walk rate, tied for the most home runs, posted their best OBP and fell just a single point off their high mark for slugging percentage in 2026. Most hitters showed marked improvement after the All-Star Break. Maybe that was the adjustment period fellow hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson, both brought on board prior to the season, needed to begin to make an impact.

Zumwalt remains Senior Director of Hitting Performance so I assume the organization hitting philosophy continues to start with him and filters down to the dugout. He will certainly be less hands-on than previously, which could be a good thing. I don't know. Also, how will the Royals ride with their hitting coaches now? Will Dawson or Thames get the bump to the lead hitting coach or will they continue in tandem? They seemed to have developed a strong working relationship with the players. The results in the last four months of the season certainly suggest some progress.

What I believe this move signals is that the Royals feel there's more to come from their offensive performance. I can't disagree there, but the club would be better served to finding two or three productive bats from outside the org. The Picollo Era has been marked by awarding too many plate appearances to too many sub-mediocre hitters.

Zumwalt has been in the sights for a segment of this fan base for the better part of two seasons. I get it. When a team underperforms—and the Royals have certainly underperformed—there needs to be accountability. Owner John Sherman's guy is Picollo. Picollo's guy is Quatraro. So someone on the coaching staff needs to take the fall. Or be reassigned.

For myself, I'm fine with this move. It needed to be made simply because the offensive valleys have been too low for too long and the peaks aren't high enough. A new voice is needed. Or the current voices—other than Zumwalt—need to be amplified. Bringing Thames and Dawson on board were solid moves. This is an opportunity to maximize the returns.

It's too bad this news broke about 24 hours before Picollo and Quatraro were scheduled to meet the media because that means we're spending a full day just speculating as to what it all means. I imagine this will be topic number one on Wednesday.

There will most certainly be more to come.

As noted earlier, MLB announced their monthly honors on Tuesday with Carter Jensen bringing home a couple of pieces of hardware. Jensen bagged the AL Player of the Month award and was also named the AL Rookie of the Month. Nice haul.

Jensen’s September was dreamy. In 21 games covering 80 PAs, he hit .338/.407/.787 with 10 doubles, eight homers and 20 RBI. Those 10 doubles were the most in the majors in September. He also led the league in extra-base hits (he tossed in one triple for good measure), slugging percentage and OPS.

I think for all of us, the most impressive part of Jensen’s month was his streak where 12 straight hits went for extra bases. That’s now a major league record for a rookie, previously held by Aaron Judge.

Just for fun—and a little perspective—I visited Stathead to find the best months in Royals history as ranked by OPS. Here are the top 15:

There are some franchise icons on that list. Impressive.

What left me kind of shocked was the note from the Royals PR team that Jensen was the first primary catcher in club history to win an AL Player of the Month award. I figure most of you will think immediately about Salvador Perez, but us elder statesmen would pivot to Darrell Porter, who had an outstanding season behind the plate for the Royals in 1979.

For fun, I took the query from Stathead above and filtered to highlight the catchers. Normally, I'd do top 10 because that's what you do. I decided to expand the list by one to help highlight the insane '79 season Porter had.

Gotta say I did not expect to see Gregg Zaun on the list. Twice!

But look at Jensen at the second-best month for a catcher in franchise history sorted by OPS. And it's the top OPS+, meaning, like wRC+ it's adjusted for league performance. He's not going to win the Rookie of the Year award, but that shouldn't diminish the impressive season he just completed. The kid is a dude.
